title: The Kuzari
hookLine: Halevi's book: a king hears a philosopher, a Christian, a Muslim and a rabbi

lines: A DREAM THAT KEEPS COMING BACK.
cards: A king wakes up from a dream he can't shake. An angel tells him: your intentions please your Creator, but your actions do not. He is sincere.
He prays, keeps his people's rituals, even serves at the altar himself. Still the dream comes back. So he summons people to explain it to him, one after another.
A few days ago we heard of a letter to a faraway king of the Khazars. Judah Halevi sets his book at the Khazar court too, with an earlier king, generations before that letter.
Today, the Kuzari: a book that begins with a man who doesn't know, and asks.

teach.b: Halevi built his book on a tradition that a king of the Khazars and some of his people took up Judaism, and he wrote it as a conversation.

The king hears a philosopher, who tells him God is far above caring about anyone's actions, and that what matters is to perfect your mind. Then a Christian scholar and a Muslim scholar each describe their faith.
Then the king calls a rabbi, and the rest of the book is their long talk.
It's Halevi's case for Judaism, written by a Jew for Jews when Jews in Spain lived as a minority among Christian and Muslim neighbors. It isn't neutral, and doesn't pretend to be.
What's striking is how the rabbi starts: not with a proof that the world was created, or an argument about God's nature, but with a story.
Put plainly: I believe in the God of Abraham, Isaac and Israel, who brought the children of Israel out of Egypt with signs and wonders, and gave them the Torah.

teach.h: BROUGHT THEE OUT OF THE LAND OF EGYPT.
teach.b: That echoes the first of the Ten Commandments, which in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation begins: "I am the LORD thy God, who brought thee out of the land of Egypt."
The point: this faith starts with a memory a people shares, not a philosopher's argument. Notice the frame, too.
The king's problem isn't belief; he's already devout. His problem is that his good intentions and his actions don't match. And the book begins because he's willing to say: I don't know.

how: The Kuzari is studied in yeshivas, adult classes and study groups as a classic of Jewish thought, often alongside the works of other medieval Jewish philosophers.

games.q: you are the king. an angel says your intentions are good but your actions are not. you are already devout. what do you do?
o: ignore the dream; you already pray.
summon teachers and ask them to explain.
change nothing and hope it stops.
games.why: the king summons a philosopher, a Christian scholar, a Muslim scholar and then a rabbi. The whole book begins because he is willing to ask.

practice: Choose one question you care about, how to raise a child or treat a difficult neighbor, and let three people you know answer it in your mind, without arguing back. Notice which answer surprises you.
If you pray, you can ask in your own words for an open mind.

wordCard.voice: The Kuzari. Judah Halevi's book in the form of a conversation: a king whose intentions are good but whose actions aren't right asks teachers, and a rabbi answers with a story. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: 'the Khazar', the name of Judah Halevi's book.

carryVoice: Your line: the king asks. A devout man, still willing to learn. See you tomorrow.
